slug: Review of Conor Kinsella's Debut as a Solo Artist in Whelan's Upstairs
title: Review of Conor Kinsella's Debut as a Solo Artist in Whelan's Upstairs
excerpt: "Fast, punchy, and had the entire place bouncing with sheer energy that I have never seen in such a confined space."
coverImageAlt: Conor Kinsella with his 6-piece band in the crowd post gig (All photos by Lydia Warfield, @35uhmm on Instagram; provided by Conor Kinsella)
author: Dylan Dowling
body: Conor Kinsella with his 6-piece band in the crowd post gig (Photo by Lydia Warfield, @35uhmm on Instagram; provided by Conor Kinsella)

The 19th of June was a very busy day in Dublin City. Metallica played their first night of two in the Aviva Stadium, and the Grand Final of the United Rugby Championship was held in Croke Park. I, however, had the absolute pleasure of being at the headliner gig of Dublin multi-instrumentalist Conor Kinsella, held upstairs in Whelan’s.
Conor Kinsella was very kind to invite myself and Barróg co-founder, Mychaela Shevlin, to the gig, and have us come and interview him ahead of his set.
Conor had two support acts on the night, bands All Girls Piss and Grá.
ꕀ ALL GIRLS PISS ꕀ
First act, punk-band All Girls Piss (AGP), label themselves as a “Post-Transexual Project”, and they were an excellent introduction to the night.

Their set was filled with influences from punk and rock music, with a lot of their music being heavy in guitars, drums and bass, and saxophone tones. The role of lead singer was shared between all members of the band, announcing before each song who wrote what; with a lot of the songs being sung by the member who wrote them.

The band themselves seemed to have excellent chemistry when playing with each other, with absolutely brilliant crowd interaction in between songs. Their stage presence seemed veteran, and every song was excellently performed with a fun energy that was exceptionally enjoyable from start to finish.

All Girls Piss have a live album called “Live From The Grand Social” that can be listened to on streaming services such as Spotify and YouTube. They also frequently do gigs around Ireland, particularly in Dublin, and I highly recommend attending if you get the chance.
ꕀ GRÁ ꕀ

Second on the bill, Irish trad/folk project Grá brought their musical talents to the Whelan's stage. On the night, Grá’s six members performed with pure excellence. Their Irish traditional sound infused with folk attributes made for an immense energy. I was at a loss for words with every song they played. With many different instruments at their disposal, namely drums, keyboards, violins and flutes they brought the entire audience in with each track.
Much like the aforementioned AGP, Grá portrayed an excellent chemistry up on stage. They made their respective roles look effortless under the lights, and it was incredible.

My favourite part of their set definitely was their closer track, a cover of the infamous Italian protest song Bella Ciao, which was absolutely awe-striking. This band feels like an unmissable experience that I am so honoured to have witnessed in person.

If you’d like to experience Grá, they play in Egan’s Aungier Street every Sunday around 6pm. They also frequently do festival spots, and have recently announced their set at Beyond The Pale later this summer. If you are planning to attend that festival, please do yourself a favour and visit their set. You will not be disappointed.
ꕀ CONOR KINSELLA ꕀ

The main act of the night, Conor Kinsella, closed the evening off with an immense six-piece band supporting him. Comprised of Alex Rosenberger “Holy Light” on drums, Daniel King on guitar, Jason Doran “Clare Hall” on bass, Cian Nolan from the band Lifts on saxophone, and Cathal Ahern on trumpet, providing incredible support for the show.

From the outset, it was clear that this set was going to be nothing short of incredible. The very first song, Stupor, was a showcase of Conor Kinsella’s musical capabilities. Everyone in the venue bore witness to how Conor used the stage to the absolute maximum, performing using keyboards, guitars, bass, and violin, sometimes at the same time!

Throughout the set there seemed to be no let up of pure energy. The second song, Tourniquet, was another example of musical excellence. At the end, Conor prompted a massive shout of the song's name (“TOURNIQUET!”) from the audience, a sound which he will use within the song’s single release later this summer.

The next song, Love Is Very Very Sad, was perhaps my favourite of the entire set. This song was fast, punchy, and had the entire place bouncing with sheer energy that I have never seen in such a confined space.

Near the end of the set, Conor shed the light on two of his guest bandmates. Alex Rosenberger’s “Holy Light”, and Jason Doran’s “Clare Hall”, with the next two songs each coming from their two solo projects respectively. A touch of class from him.

Before the encore, which Conor dedicated to his late grandmother, he finished with a performance of his brand new single, SOMEONEUKNOW. After listening to the single multiple times in the lead-up to the gig, I was curious to see how Conor would convert this energy to a live stage setting. Conor and his band absolutely blew it out of the park, playing an exceptional performance of his new single that got the crowd rocking yet again.
ꕀ INTERVIEW WITH CONOR KINSELLA ꕀ

Before the gig, I got the opportunity to interview Conor Kinsella about the themes surrounding his new song “SOMEONEUKNOW”, his creative framework, his support set for ‘Crywank’ last January, and his love for collaborating with musicians.
How are you feeling ahead of the gig?

Conor: I’m not nervous at all. I’m like, pretty excited actually. Once I got through the sound check, it sounds so different to a rehearsal room when you have a proper sound engineer and it feels kind of larger than life. I think it’s going to be a really special night tonight.
You released your latest single "SOMEONEUKNOW" on Monday [15.06.2026], What were the themes surrounding the writing of the song and where did it come from?

Conor: Sure, so there was kind of two things. I’ve been trying to think about my music in a  more politicised way the past two years, because I spent a very long time writing pop songs, and I think that’s a very good thing to do if you’re any kind of musician, but I wanted to start writing stuff that kind of reflects the state of the world a little bit more. I’m from Dublin and I grew up here but I always remember whenever you would pass the front of the Dail on the bus and you’d see far-right campaigners shouting about booting all immigrants out of the  country and that sort of thing. So I just wanted to write something, especially it was crazy seeing that song came out maybe like ten days after what happened in Belfast [2026 Belfast Riots] and stuff, but I felt like it was kind of cathartic to make my own sort of ideas about it in my head about what’s going on, because you look somewhere like the US and how bad things are over there. You think that could never happen here, but it already exists in a way.
Is this political theming something you want to explore in future releases? Do you feel like you have more to say on the matter?

Conor: Yeah for sure. You’ll see it when you come into the set tonight, but one of the songs I wrote is about what’s happening in Palestine and specifically like how governments in the West have ignored what’s going on there just for the sake of continuing economic ties with Israel. There has been so much talk about trying to get the Occupied Territories Bill passed and it’s just constantly pushed down the road because I don’t think any Fianna Fáil or Fine Gael government is ever gonna have the courage to do that y’know? And then even in terms of other things, there’s an artificial intelligence love song in there tonight too. So yeah, I’d say a lot of what I’m writing about at the minute is reflective of things that maybe a lot of people are feeling in today’s world but aren’t sure how to articulate their thoughts about. That’s what most of my songs are, just me trying to get my own ideas straight about how I feel about all this stuff.
Just to get back to music and performance, I’ve seen that you supported CRYWANK in January in Dublin. What was that like for you, and what did it teach you about performance?

Conor: That was a pretty crazy gig because that was also the second ever gig that we did with this project [Conor Kinsella]. I got the call for that gig from a promoter, shoutout nvr.mnt promotions! that I know from my last band [Speakers] and he just asked if I had my next thing in the works and I thought that if this is the type of opportunity that’s there, we’ll make it work. That was just an incredible show, it felt kind of surreal to be suddenly just going up on stage only maybe half an hour after doors and the place was packed out y’know? So it was quite intimidating in a way, because I think when you play gigs in Dublin you’re not necessarily used to that level of immediate enthusiasm from an audience, but that room was like, packed way to the back before we even got on stage. I got to talk to Jay and other members (of CRYWANK) too and they’re so nice. They’re proper seasoned touring artists. In terms of what it taught me, I don’t know, just like keep pushing because it was kind of mad to do something like that right out the gate. It gave me confidence to just keep trying new stuff, ‘cause what I’m doing is so different to what I’ve historically kind of done. You don’t know how people are going to react but the audience reaction to every single show so far has been so kind. Everyone has been really nice about it.

With this project, you’ve been starting to work with a lot more new people, and getting a lot more creative voices on your work. Is this something you like doing, and is this something you’ve learned a lot from?

Conor: Completely. When I first had the bones of my first single SOMEONEUKNOW together back in March of last year I was like “aw, this really needs a saxophone on it”. I went to meet some friends from college and there was a few people there who I wouldn’t have known as well but I was just talking to one of them, this guy Sultan, and he just mentioned in passing that he played the saxophone. I was like, “Oh, would you be interested in listening to a track and seeing what you make of it?”. And he was so modest about his skills which was crazy. I don’t know if you’ve heard the song yet, but it's like the craziest saxophone stuff ever! So that was the first part of that single, and from there I was like “Oh I’d love to have a little bit of cello on there too!” and I’m fortunate enough that one of my good friends is an amazing cello player. So I went down to her house in Cork for a night,I took some microphones with me and I just turned her living room into a studio for a couple of hours. I am literally down to work with anyone who plays an instrument that I don’t already have a little bit of a handle on unless they’re like, I don’t know, I’m trying to think who’s like the best guitar player in the world… if Geordie Greep (Black Midi) said “I wanna play guitar on one of your songs”, I’d be like “yes please!”. But the main thing with this stuff is unusual instruments, stuff that you wouldn’t typically see in a rock band. Even tonight, you’ll see with the support acts (All Girls Piss, Grá) they both kind of, they make sort of rock-adjacent music, but it’s got these extra dimensions with saxophones, flutes and violins and all this other stuff in there. It really changes the flavour of the music in a way that’s just very cool. Maybe in a few years I’ll just want to go back to writing for just guitar, bass, drums and vocals, but right now I’m really enjoying the textural aspect of making this stuff and seeing what other people think of it. Even my idea of a trumpet line for a song might be weird since I don’t play the trumpet, but someone else will come and say “well this doesn’t work, no trumpet player in their right mind would ever play this”. And then Cathal (Aherne), who’s playing trumpet with me tonight, he’ll come in and he’ll just flesh out something and I’ll be like “aw that’s really good! I never would have thought of that”. So that’s kind of the beauty of it in a way, that you just get to bring in so many different perspectives about music and just see what other people think of what you’ve made.
